title: Short Stuff: Scheele's Green
summary: Short Stuff episode on Scheele's green, the bright copper-arsenic pigment created by Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Covers how the arsenic-laden color became a Victorian craze in clothing, soap, food, toys, wallpaper and stamps; the 1861 death of artificial flower maker Matilda Scheer, which prompted Parliament to regulate arsenic in food; the theory that Napoleon's exile wallpaper contributed to his death; and the 1950s case of Clare Boothe Luce, ambassador to Italy, whose bedroom wallpaper was linked to arsenic poisoning. Part one of a two-part series on color.

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode about a color, the first of a two-part series on accidental color history.

segments.title: Who was Carl Wilhelm Scheele
segments.summary: Introduction of Scheele's green, named after German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele, and its brilliant color that was also toxic.

segments.title: Discovery of the pigment
segments.summary: Scheele made the pigment by heating sodium carbonate, adding arsenious oxide and copper sulfate. He reportedly knew it was toxic and worried about it in a letter to a friend, per Victoria Finley's account.

segments.title: Arsenic as a murder poison
segments.summary: Arsenic was long known as a poison, with nonspecific symptoms that made it useful for murder until the Marsh test by James Marsh in 1830.

segments.title: Acute vs long-term arsenic poisoning
segments.summary: Symptoms of acute arsenic poisoning like vomiting, diarrhea, and numbness could be mistaken for other causes. Long-term exposure causes skin lesions, patchy hard skin and cancer. Scheele's green spread the awareness of long-term harm.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before discussing the pigment's popularity.

segments.title: Scheele's green craze
segments.summary: The green took the world by storm and appeared in clothing, soap, food, beauty products, stamps, wallpaper and children's toys, especially in smoggy Victorian London. A brief pedantic aside about the Costanza reference.

segments.title: Why the green was so popular
segments.summary: The green was a vibrant, saturated middle green, unlike the duller copper-based greens before it, and people loved it.

segments.title: Matilda Scheer's death and regulation
segments.summary: Reports emerged of illness among women and children; A. W. Hofmann estimated a headpiece had enough arsenic to poison twenty people. The 1861 death of 19-year-old artificial flower maker Matilda Scheer, who had inhaled and ingested the pigment, spurred public concern and Parliament regulated arsenic in food within about ten years.

segments.title: Napoleon and the wallpaper theory
segments.summary: Some believe Napoleon's exile on Saint Helena, with green wallpaper and damp conditions, released arsenic dust that may have contributed to his stomach cancer.

segments.title: Clare Boothe Luce arsenic poisoning
segments.summary: In the 1950s, ambassador Clare Boothe Luce in Italy had arsenic poisoning. The CIA investigated, and her bedroom ceiling was found to contain arsenic, released by a rattling washing machine upstairs.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank sources and sign off with a short joke about a listener's Schloss green headdress, followed by the show credit.
